Chapter 2: The Power of a Few — How Certain People Start Social Epidemics
Have you ever noticed there’s always that one person in your community who just seems to know everyone? Maybe they’re the friend who connects you with a new job opportunity, or the one who always recommends the best spot for dinner. Somehow, they always seem to hear the latest news before anyone else.
These kinds of people quietly play a huge role in how ideas and trends catch on.
Imagine a neighborhood where a brand new café just opened. At first, things are pretty quiet. But then, one day, someone who’s a regular at the local gym stops in for coffee. She chats with the barista, tries a pastry, and leaves with a big smile. Later on, she mentions the café to a few friends at her yoga class. By the end of the week, that once-empty café is suddenly packed. The owner is left wondering—what changed? The answer: one person set off a whole chain reaction.
This is what’s known as the Law of the Few. The idea here is simple: just a small group of people can have a massive impact on how things spread. Not everyone is equally influential. Some folks are natural connectors—they jump easily between different groups, bringing people together. Others are what we call mavens—they love gathering and sharing all kinds of information. And then, you’ve got the salesmen—the ones whose enthusiasm and charm make you want to listen, and maybe even follow their lead.
Let’s talk about connectors for a moment. They’re really the social glue in any community. They remember names, they love making introductions, and they’re always building bridges between people who might never have met otherwise. Their contact lists are like treasure troves, full of people from every walk of life. When a connector hears about something new, it doesn’t take long before that news is everywhere.
Now, mavens are a little different. They’re detail lovers. They notice the difference between two brands of cereal, track down the best deals, and genuinely enjoy sharing what they’ve found. People trust mavens—not because they’re extra charming, but because they really know their stuff. When a maven recommends something, you can bet others are listening.
Then there are the salesmen. They bring a whole different kind of energy. Their enthusiasm is contagious, and they know how to persuade without ever coming off as pushy. When a salesman gets excited about something, it’s almost impossible not to get swept up with them.
What’s amazing is how these three types—connectors, mavens, and salesmen—often work together, without even realizing it, to get social epidemics started. Maybe a connector hears about a cool new idea from a maven, then shares it with dozens of their friends. A salesman picks up the idea and spreads it even further, convincing the skeptics to give it a shot.
Here’s a real-world example. Think about a new children’s show that’s struggling to find an audience. The producers reach out to a handful of parents who are plugged into their communities. Those parents, acting as connectors, start sharing the show with their networks. A few mavens write detailed reviews, explaining what makes the show different. And the salesmen? They talk up the show at school events and playdates. Pretty soon, what started as a small project turns into a hit, with the audience growing faster than anyone expected.
Most people miss just how powerful these few individuals can be. They imagine trends spreading evenly, like water filling up a glass. But in reality? The process is a lot more uneven—and a lot more surprising. One connector can do more to spread an idea than a hundred other people. A maven’s recommendation can matter more than a national ad campaign. And a salesman’s pitch can turn even the biggest skeptic into a fan.
So, here’s the key takeaway: when you want to spark real change, it’s not about reaching everyone. It’s about finding the right people—the connectors, the mavens, and the salesmen—who have the power to tip the balance. These folks are the hidden engines behind social epidemics, turning tiny sparks into roaring fires.
